_areas_note: One road end serves this zone: the Baker River trailhead at 775 ft, at the very end of the Baker Lake road (FS 11), roughly 25.5 miles up from the highway. Trail 606 crosses the Baker River on a suspension bridge about ten minutes in and enters North Cascades National Park; the climbers' path for Blum leaves the trail within a couple of hundred yards of that bridge and grinds 4,000 vertical feet up the forested spur north of Blum Creek to the Blum Lakes. Hagan is climbed off those same lakes, over the ridge running southeast from them, so it shares the approach and the camps exactly. TWO PEAKS WERE REMOVED AFTER CHECKING THEIR REAL APPROACHES. Bacon Peak does not go from the Baker River trail at all: parties reach it either from the Anderson and Watson Lakes trailhead at the end of the Anderson Creek road (FS 1107), a completely separate spur off the Baker Lake road that climbs to 4,200 ft on the far side of Baker Lake, or from the end of the Bacon Creek road on the highway near Marblemount for the Diobsud Creek Glacier line. Its camps are the Anderson, Watson and Diobsud lakes, in the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, under a different agency and a different permit regime — nothing in this file applies to it. Berdeen Peak likewise belongs to the Bacon Creek road: the documented ascent starts at 850 ft at the road end and bushwhacks up Porkbelly Ridge to the peak's east ridge, camping above Berdeen Lake, which drains east into Bacon Creek rather than west toward Baker Lake. It can be reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the Blum-Hagan col, but that is a traverse variation, not its approach. THIS IS A ZONE WITH ALMOST NO ESTABLISHED CAMPING and the file says so plainly rather than manufacturing sites: there is one designated camp on the valley trail, a handful of tent-sized shelves at the Blum Lakes, heather benches on the Hagan side, and otherwise nothing. ROAD STATUS IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK — as of summer 2026 the Baker Lake road is closed just past Shannon Creek Campground near milepost 23, to vehicles and to foot travel, which cuts off this trailhead entirely.

sites.name: Lower Blum Lake
sites.capacity: Two or three small tents on heather shelves and gravel near the outlet; the basin is tight and the park caps this cross-country zone at six people and two parties at a time
sites.water: The lake itself, and a small outlet stream. Treat everything. This is the first reliable water since the river, four thousand feet below
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required year-round for any overnight stay. The Blum cross-country zone is not one of the reservable zones, so it is walk-up only through the wilderness information center near Marblemount. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow, and keep a hundred feet back from the water. Human waste goes in a cathole or, on snow and glacier, in a blue bag carried out. Bear canisters are the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from, and can be borrowed in person at the permit office
sites.notes: This is the base camp for both peaks and effectively the only one. Getting here is the whole difficulty of the trip: leave trail 606 a short distance past the Baker River suspension bridge, before Blum Creek, and find the faint path that works away from the creek through old timber. The first section is genuine devil's club, fern and deadfall bushwhacking, and the path comes and goes; above that it settles into a steep, tiring forest ridge, then an ascending traverse along the south side of that ridge into the lake basin. Five hours from the car is a good day, and parties routinely take longer. For Mount Blum, the south ridge and southeast slopes go from here up through gullies and snow to the east ridge. For Hagan, climb southeast from the lower lake to about 5,600 ft on the east-west ridge, then traverse south toward the pass below the Hagan peaks. Best from mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse to the lakes is a snow slope with a long runout, later and the water thins. There is no shelter of any kind and no cell coverage.

sites.name: Middle Blum Lake
sites.capacity: One or two tents on the benches above the shore; smaller and more exposed than the lower lake
sites.permit: Same North Cascades National Park backcountry permit and the same Blum zone rules as the lower lake — walk-up only, six people, no fires, durable surfaces, hundred-foot setback from water
sites.notes: A few hundred yards and a hundred feet of gain above the lower lake, and the more common choice for parties who want to shorten summit day on Blum. The ground is heather and slab, so tent sites are where the rock is, not where the flat grass is. It holds snow later than the lower lake and it catches more wind, which is a fair trade for mosquitoes in July. From here the line to Blum's summit continues past the upper tarn and into the gullies below the east ridge, and the Hagan traverse also starts from this shelf. Nothing about the position changes the approach problem — you still spend a full day getting up from the river.

sites.name: Upper Blum tarn, southeast of the main lakes
sites.capacity: One or two tents at most, on rock and gravel; there is no established site here, only ground that happens to work
sites.water: The tarn, when it is out; it is snow-covered well into summer and may be a snowpatch rather than water in early season. Carry from the lakes below if in doubt
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, Blum cross-country zone, walk-up only. No fires. Because this sits above the meadow line, expect to be camping on snow or bare rock, which is what the zone rules ask for anyway
sites.notes: The highest practical ground on the Blum side, on the way from the main lakes toward the gullies and snow slopes leading to Blum's east ridge. It buys perhaps an hour on summit day and costs an extra 700 ft of carrying at the end of an already brutal approach day, so most parties leave it to those going on to Hagan or continuing the traverse east. Exposed to weather from every direction. In a low-snow year the tarn is dry and this stops being an option at all.

sites.name: South Hagan bench
sites.capacity: Two tents on heather and gravel benches; informal, with no fixed site
sites.water: Snowmelt runnels and small pools that shrink through the season; late summer parties should plan to carry water up from the Blum Lakes or from Hidden Lake below
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This ground sits on the boundary between the Blum and Bacon Peak cross-country zones, so confirm which zone your permit is written for when you pick it up. Six-person party limit either way, no fires, no camping in meadow
sites.notes: Open benches on the south side of Hagan Mountain, reached from the Blum Lakes by climbing to the ridge crest near 5,600 ft and traversing south. This is where parties stage for Hagan's south slopes: from the bench, talus and a scree couloir lead to the southwest end of the Hagan crags, and slabs on the south side give the final scramble to the summit. It is also the natural stop for anyone continuing east toward Hidden Lake and Bacon. The bench is comfortable and the position is superb, but it is fully exposed and the water is seasonal, which is the reason most parties still base at the lakes and do Hagan in a long day.

sites.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
sites.capacity: Two or three tents on the flats near the shore
sites.water: The lake. Treat it. Reliable all season, which is not true of the benches above
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This lake sits toward the Bacon Peak side of the divide, so check which cross-country zone the ranger writes your permit for. No fires, six-person limit, camp a hundred feet back from the water
sites.notes: A small lake in the saddle country between Hagan and Bacon, reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the ridge southeast of them and dropping to it. It matters here as the reliable water on Hagan's far side and as the standard second night for parties traversing east. It is a considerable drop below the Hagan bench, so it is a poor choice if Hagan is your only objective — you give back four hundred feet you will re-climb in the morning. Reaching it involves snow into midsummer and steep heather afterwards. Do not treat this as an approach camp for Bacon Peak from the Baker River side; the practical way to Bacon is from a different road entirely.

sites.name: Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
sites.capacity: Two established sites and a backcountry toilet; a small party each
sites.water: Sulphide Creek and the Baker River, both close by. Treat the water; the river runs silty in high melt
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a designated camp, which is a different reservation than a cross-country zone — book it or ask for it at the permit office rather than assuming a zone permit covers it. No fires
sites.notes: This is the only designated, built camp anywhere near this trailhead: flat sites and a toilet at the end of trail 606, a couple of easy valley miles past the suspension bridge. IT IS NOT ON THE WAY TO BLUM OR HAGAN. The climbers' path for both peaks leaves the trail near Blum Creek, well before this, and heading up-valley to Sulphide takes you in the wrong direction. It is listed because it is the legal, comfortable option for a party that arrives late, wants a short first evening, or is waiting out weather at the bottom, and because low-elevation valley ground here is otherwise wet, brushy and off-limits. Elevation is valley-bottom, only a little above the trailhead.

sites.name: Blum Creek spur ridge, forest bivy
sites.capacity: One tent, found rather than chosen; the ridge is steep, timbered and littered with deadfall, and genuinely flat ground is rare
sites.water: None dependable. Blum Creek is below the path and hard to reach from the ridge; carry what you need from the river or push on to the lakes
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit if you sleep here — the park boundary sits close to the river crossing, so assume the whole climb is inside the park and ask at the permit office where the line actually falls before you plan on it. No fires
sites.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMP ON THIS APPROACH, and this entry exists to say so honestly rather than to recommend a place. The 4,000 ft of steep forest between the Baker River and the Blum Lakes has no benches worth the name, no water on the crest and no clearings; parties who run out of daylight here flatten a spot among the trees and move on at first light. The right plan is to start early and reach the lakes in one push. Keep it in mind only as what you will actually do if the bushwhacking at the bottom eats more of the day than you expected, which it often does in wet conditions, or if somebody in the party is struggling with the load.
